content_html_sanitized:
Posted April 23, 2002
See

On Thursday, the NORML weekly press release will undoubtedly report on the 2002 Conference in San Francisco; however, I left this one more optimistic than ever.

There were great speeches by SF District Attorney Terence Hallinan and defense attorney Tony Serra, and many others -- and great panels on a variety of subjects.

I chaired a panel on developments outside of DEAland, the highlight of which was a report from New Zealand by Chris Fowlie, the head of NZ NORML. I am very glad that I added him to the schedule.

Amazingly, his trip was financed -- unintentionally -- by a NZ newspaper that paid him for having falsely reported that he had been put in jail, when he was arrested for cannabis possession. (He was ultimately acquitted in a landmark case that will inhibit the NZ police's ability to stop people arbitrarily on suspicion of cannabis possession.)

Can you imagine how easy it would be to finance reform if DEAland papers paid us every time they lied to their readers about cannabis!

Critical mass

Although there were over 520 people there, the most to ever attend a NORML conference, it was the quality of the people, notably the students, that I found most encouraging. And as much as I enjoyed seeing old friends, it was really great meeting so many new ones. I think that the movement is growing to the point where we are reaching " critical mass " the size needed for a chain reaction in growth.

But, it is in quality not just quantity that we need to be critical.

Perspective and moral concerns

In the 30 years since I attended NORML's " First People's Pot Conference " in an old church in Washington, DC, NORML has had its ups and downs. Now is definitely an " up " time.

Much of the credit for this progress has to go to Allen St. Pierre, the head of the NORML Foundation. He is not only the hardest worker that I have ever known, he is an absolute moral compass in my life, the importance of which you will understand better in a moment.

However, from the beginning it has also been NORML founder Keith Stroup's vision that NORML would act as an umbrella organization for the marijuana reform movement. Keith is an old pro -- and a very dear old friend -- and he really tries to work with everyone in the movement. I understand and admire that.

This conference illustrated that beautifully, with an occasional bizarre twist.

For example, the relationship between NORML and Ed Rosenthal has long been strained.
See

But when Rosenthal was arrested for his alleged involvement in supplying a California medical marijuana club, Keith had no hesitancy about giving him a place on the program to tell his story.

An even more remarkable example of Keith's commitment to collegiality and cooperation is the fact that he tries to work with Rob Kampia, the founder of MPP. Kampia paid to attend and mostly worked the lobby. Fair enough, however

When I was National Director of NORML, I gave Kampia his first job, and then I fired him. No big deal, but after I fired him, he falsely claimed that the reason that I fired him was that he objected to marijuana smoking in the NORML office. As it happens, that was not true, but true or not, narking is the one unforgivable sin in my book. So this will be one of the few times that you will find any mention of him on MarijuanaNews.com

However, far from making him a pariah in the movement, he was immediately backed by some of the other groups, and over the years received crucial funding from the Soros organization. Now he even gets to veto funding for NORML from these groups.

In fact, he has long been waging war on NORML with the help of some of the leaders of the broader anti-prohibitionist movement. They want the marijuana reform movement subsumed into their " harm-reduction " agenda. Notice that while NORML's web site header is " working to reform the marijuana laws " and NORML says, " Stop arresting responsible marijuana users, " the MPP site header is simply " Working to minimize the harm associated with marijuana. " Of course, George Bush might make the same claim!

I am not at all opposed to " harm-reduction " -- but the legalization of cannabis is a separate issue, vitally important in its own right. We should not hide behind " harm reduction " nor should we tolerate being used by closet smokers who won't stand up for the cannabis community.

Nonetheless, the " harm-reduction " crowd dominates the broader anti-prohibitionist movement thanks to the major funders, one of whom (not Soros) is now funding MPP. How a billionaire who has been arrested for marijuana possession can fund someone who has narked NORML is beyond my comprehension. That is his problem, but now it is also a problem for the integrity of the movement.

This is the first time that I have ever written about this, and it may seem odd that I would do so in this context, but all that we have going for us is the truth. We have the moral high ground precisely because we are not like the narks.

Having been at this as long as I have, and having seen the damage that infighting has done the movement, I am very reluctant to be " negative. " Certainly, there will be knowledgeable people in the movement who would prefer that I not bring this up, as much as they may agree and most do. (I might add that no one at NORML had anything to do with my writing this.) And certainly, there is so much more that I will never talk about, especially about Kampia.

However, when I met so many fine young people at this conference, I felt that I could no longer remain silent about this.

Some may work with MPP, out of a sense of collegiality, as does my friend Keith. And certainly now that MPP has money to distribute for worthwhile causes, there is no reason for others not to try to work with them, but everyone should do so with their eyes open.

We are winning, and when we have won, there will be many who will try to take the credit for the victory, and some who will deserve at least a part of it. However, Allen St. Pierre, in spite of all that he has done, will not be out there putting his face all over a web site. He will not even be taking credit for a fraction of what he has accomplished.

But we will have won because we are transcendently right, and there are so many people like Allen who are simply committed to doing what is right, no matter who gets the credit.

And that is the most important strategic insight of all.
